utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis without Judge Lattanzi. She is indisposed today. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could introduce to the Trial Chamber Elena Gencheua of Bulgaria who is one of our legal interns who is sitting in during this session. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I wanted to raise one matter in connection with the anticipated testimony of Mr. Milosevic next week, who, as the Court is aware, is a significant Defence witness whose testimony is expected to cover a considerable amount of ground. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a note in response to Mr. Robinson's suggestion, that does raise -- by itself it raises certain logistical issues that would concern us to change the order, but more importantly it neglects the overriding issue of the translation of the documents which is a significant matter for us by way of preparation. utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we start with the next witness, you could try that well in advance with respect to other witnesses, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think proofing a witness by sending him written questions and getting written answers through his counsel is really not a very satisfactory way to do it because you want to ask questions based on the answers that they give you. So, I mean, it's one way to collect some information, but we don't believe that it's a good way to do it and we would prefer to go to the location where the witness is with the witness's lawyer, conduct a producer proofing, and then prepare a 92 ter statement. And we don't see why that can't be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, I take it it could save some time at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It could save some time, but it would also take an inordinate amount of time to prepare the questions, run them by the counsel, prepare the answers, run those by the counsel, and then finally get the final result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it there. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, you will be testifying today under the protective measures of pseudonym and image distortion. Do you understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D7102 without broadcasting of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: KW570

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be tendered under seal, KW570.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit D2769, admitted under seal, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 1D06277.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement you have given to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: It should be signed at the bottom, sir. It is, indeed. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: KW570

utterances.speaker: KW570

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I now tender this statement under Rule 92 ter and also the redacted part that we've discussed, under seal of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we will admit Rule 92 ter statement under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit D2770, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can the redacted version of his diary be admitted publicly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, because it does at the very top reveal information that would lead to disclosing his identity. So we would ask that those two associated exhibits be both admitted under seal and we would also ask that they be added to our 65 ter list as this witness was added after the 65 ter list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. No objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that request is granted and we'll admit both as Exhibit D2771 and 2772 under seal. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to read the summary of Witness KW570 in English. I will read slowly for the sake of the interpreters. [In English] Witness KW570 was deployed to the former Yugoslavia from January until June 1994 as a member of UNPROFOR. Witness KW570 will testify that the Serbs were already being blamed for the Markale market explosion on 5th of February, 1994, before any investigation was completed. He found it highly unusual that the Serbs would have fired a single round at the market-place. Normally, the Serbs fired several rounds when seeking to hit a target with their mortars. Given the height of the buildings and their proximity to the place where the shell landed in the market, it appeared that the shell would have had to come with a very high trajectory, suggesting that it had been fired at close range. Major John Russell, an artillery officer who served as military assistant to civilian affairs director Sergio De Mello went to the scene on the 5th of February, 1994, and stated that he was surprised that shrapnel and other physical evidence could not be found at the scene and may have been removed. Witness KW570 noted this in his diary in an entry for 7th of February, 1994, where he added that "the whole thing was a bit suspicious, the whole world was still blaming the Serbs despite lack of evidence." UNPROFOR also received information that the shell may have been fired by a Mujahedin group who allegedly missed their target when trying to kill Jews who were leaving Sarajevo at the same time. At a meeting between General Rose and VRS Chief of Staff General Milovanovic at Lukavica barracks on 6th of February, 1994, General Milosevic adamantly -- Milovanovic adamantly denied that the Serbs had fired the shell which landed on the market and offered personally to go to Sarajevo to assist in the investigation of the shelling. On 8th of February, 1994, a meeting was held between General Rose and the leadership of the Bosnian military in Sarajevo. The Bosnian government forces were represented by Generals Divjak, Hajrulahovic, and Colonel Dakic. During the meeting, General Rose said that evidence was emerging that the market-place shelling may have been carried out by their side. There was complete silence after he made this statement. They then produced a number of excuses, which included a claim that they had taped a conversation involving the Serbs to the effect that they had confessed to the atrocity. However, the Bosnian government never produced any such tape nor evidence to demonstrate that the Serbs had fired the mortar. The next day when the Bosnian military delegation refused to take part in meetings to arrange a cease-fire, General Rose once again met with the Bosnian government leadership. He told them that unless they participated in the meetings he would tell the world what he suspected about the shelling of the market-place. The Bosnian government then agreed to participate in the meetings. All of these circumstances led Witness KW570 to believe that in all probability it was probably not the Serbs who fired the shell at the Markale market. It was his experience in Sarajevo that the Bosnian government pursued a strategy of trying to blame Serbs for atrocities in order to obtain international intervention on their side. Examples for this were the outgoing fire of mortars from hospitals, schools, and other civilian areas, and from areas adjacent to United Nations positions, which would draw return fire from the Serbs into those areas. Throughout the subsequent cease-fire for Sarajevo signed by both sides, the Bosnian government military were guilty of the vast majority of the breaches of its terms. The Bosnian government refused to approve a water system established by American humanitarian activist Fred Cuny on the pretext that the water was not clean enough, because the government did not want to alleviate the suffering of civilians in Sarajevo. Witness KW570 attended meetings at which Radovan Karadzic was present on many occasions during his time in Bosnia and spoke on the telephone with Dr. Karadzic several times. He found Dr. Karadzic to be polite and easy to work with. He observed that Dr. Karadzic appeared to be a moderating influence on other members of the Bosnian Serb political leadership and the Bosnian Serb military. Dr. Karadzic often tried to satisfy the demands of the international community. [Interpretation] That would be the summary, and for the time being I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as you have noted that your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in its entirety and you will be now cross-examined by a member of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when we met on 7 January of this year, at that time I gave you an electronic copy of an information report that had been prepared by a former staff member here at the Tribunal as a result of a meeting with you in 1997. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please call up that information report and of course not broadcast it. It's 65 ter number 24420. Could we just go over to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you recognise here, Mr. Witness, the document that we provided you with in January during our meeting in January?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I do recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the service in Bosnia and Herzegovina you mentioned in your statement to Dr. Karadzic's Defence, this document also mentions a further deployment or your initial deployment to the area from November 1992 to May 1993 as part of the British contingent with UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this document also discusses the market-place shelling of 5 February 1994. It details some meetings and negotiations following the incident to achieve a cease-fire and establish and implement the total exclusion zone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It also talks about the situation in Gorazde in April 1994, and I'll just list some of the other topics. Negotiations for cease-fires in the area, the sequence of events surrounding the air-strikes that month, the detention of UN peacekeepers and UNMOs following the air-strikes, your mission to Gorazde as part of the United Nations in the implementation of the eventual cease-fire there, and your travel in June of 1994 to Geneva during further negotiations following the incident. Do I have that, in essence, correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And during our interview, you reviewed this document and found -- and commented that you found the information that was set out there to be accurate as far as you recalled; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could please move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we do that, Mr. President, we would object to any questions about this incident as being beyond the scope of direct examination and not related to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your basis is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our basis is that the cross-examination is limited to the scope of the direct examination and issues of credibility, and we don't think that the issue of his activity in 1993, which is -- arises from the statement or is related to his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence. With respect, Your Honour, of course we're entitled to do that. I mean, this is -- this is -- under Rule 90(H), we are entitled to put our case -- put our case to the witness. I could go further, but I think it's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if they want to do that, first of all, they have to put their case to the witness which hasn't been done. But secondly, it's our position that on -- that the Prosecution cannot, during the Defence case, elicit evidence which it didn't elicit during its case in chief, and therefore improve -- offer additional evidence through the Defence case that's not related to the subject of the witness's testimony or his credibility. So it's our position that essentially the Prosecution is limited during the Defence case to the materials that are relevant to the witness's testimony or to his credibility and is not allowed to improve its case by questioning Defence witnesses on unrelated topics. And if they do do that, if you do allow them to do that, then they have to put their case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, if you read Rule 90(H)(i): "The cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of that case," and their putting the case is limited to (ii) where the cross-examining is putting some contradictory evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the way I read -- on your second point, the way I read (ii) is in that third category of evidence described in (i), "where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case of the cross-examining party," then in that case the "counsel shall put to the witness the nature of the case of the party," although it does say "which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." So it appears to me that either they have to put their case to the witness in the question or that the witness's testimony has to be contradictory to the case of the -- they have to have evidence contradictory to the witness's testimony in order to even elicit evidence under the third part of number 1, which is relevant to their case. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we need to stay in private session for this debate. Shall we continue in private session? Yes, Ms. Edgerton, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the end of the day when we receive the transcript, I can review the transcript and mark what could be in public session. Not really, Your Honours, with respect to adding anything. These are two completely separate provisions and (ii) doesn't modify (i) at all. I would submit we're -- this man has evidence relevant to the case; it's related to evidence that has come before Your Honours and we should be entitled to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what is your response to Mr. Robinson's, albeit belated -- shall we go back to open session, albeit for a brief moment? Could the Chamber move back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can lift the confidentiality from line 5 of transcript page 25. If you have any other opinion, please let us know. My question for you, Ms. Edgerton, is: What do you think about Mr. Robinson's statement that or argument that the Prosecution cannot during the Defence case elicit evidence which it didn't elicit during its case in chief and therefore improve or offer additional evidence through the Defence case that's not related to the subject of the witness's testimony or his credibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can address that, Mr. President, since it seems to be a slightly wider issue. Let me say, first of all, that the proposition advanced by Mr. Robinson now is completely at odds with the position they took during the course of the Prosecution case when it served their interest to read 90(H) in just the manner we're advancing now, which is the correct reading of that. 90(H)(i) talks about what you can elicit properly so because it's relevant information. 90(H)(ii) talks about the obligation of a cross-examiner to make sure that he or she puts the case to the witness so that you're not dancing around the edges and the witness is given an opportunity to address that part of the case. Two quite separate provisions as indicated by the very language, one of which talks about what can be elicited and one of which talks about the responsibilities of the examiner. Beyond that the suggestion -- first of all, there's a little apples and oranges here. Obviously it's impossible to elicit from a witness who hasn't been called evidence related to particular aspects of the case, and so there has been jurisprudence which talks about the limited circumstances in which the Prosecution in this case is -- may be precluded from leading certain evidence that was it wasn't -- that it was in a position to advance in the course of its case, that it failed to do, and the extent of any prejudice it may cause the accused, but to suggest that the Prosecution cannot lead from a witness called by the Defence evidence about matters that were advanced and were discussed and were at issue throughout the course of the case is specious and is at odds with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and I'm sure the experience of this Bench, in previous cases. It has -- it's illogical. It would preclude the Chamber from hearing the information which witnesses brought before this Chamber have that illuminate issues in the case. It cannot possibly be a matter that goes to notice or prejudice because the witness is called by the -- by the Defence. And any suggestion along the lines advanced by Mr. Robinson would be inimical to the interests of justice and would unfairly constrain the information available to this Court which it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, there's actually jurisprudence on this issue from the Appeals Chamber. Unfortunately my internet isn't working fast enough. But in the Prlic case there's a decision on the interlocutory appeal against the Trial Chamber's decision on the presentation of documents by the Prosecution in cross-examination of Defence witnesses. It's dated the 26th of February, 2009. I am not able to call up that decision but I have my notes, and the Appeals Chamber did put some limitations on the right of the Prosecution or ability to elicit evidence on cross-examination of matters other than what was covered by the direct or credibility. So if -- either if we can pass this issue until the next recess or take a recess early, I think we would all benefit from being able to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, as regards the provision in Rule 90(H)(ii) which refers to the putting the case to the witness, apart from whether I would agree with it or not, is it not related to the common practice where the parties can -- is stopped from arguing something unless it puts to the witness who could have answered the question? So it's a bit different from the perspective of Rule 90(H)(i), isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Judge Morrison is in the best position to answer that question because the Americans don't use that putting your case business, but the English certainly do. But I think that you're correct, that was the purpose of Rule -- of (ii), but it does seem to modify or at least it applies to the third part of (i). So although it may have had that purpose, the issue is still whether or not that's a limitation which applies to any time a cross-examining party wants to ask a witness about things that are outside of credibility and the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the importance of the issue, to make a more informed decision the Chamber will rise for 40 minutes and resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, Judge Lattanzi is now sitting with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, may I introduce one more member of our team and that is Francie Derderyan from Armenia who is a legal intern with our team and is joining us during this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope the courtroom is warm enough for Judge Lattanzi. The Chamber observes that it adopted a consistent practice during the Prosecution case with respect to the interpretation of Rule 90(H) which allowed the Defence to adduce evidence relevant to his case during his cross-examination within the meaning of Rule 90(H). The Chamber's prima facie reading of the rule and the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence cited by Mr. Robinson is that Rule 90(H) does not preclude the Prosecution from doing the same during their cross-examination of Defence witnesses. If fresh evidence is being adduced, the Chamber will exercise control over the admission of such evidence on a case-by-case basis to ensure that the interest of justice and the interest of the accused are protected. That said, however, separate from the requirements of Rule 90(H)(ii), the Chamber considers that it would be very kind of the Prosecution to inform of the subject matter if it is minded to put questions not related to the subject matter of the -- in the evidence in chief for the benefit of witness, parties, and Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, of course, Your Honours, and I -- if I can go back up in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, probably you were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, not at all. I enumerated some of those when we talked about the contents of the document 65 ter number 24420 which remains on the screen in front of us. So the topics, if I may, are the initial -- issues related to the initial deployment of the witness in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, in particular Eastern Bosnia; the situation in Sarajevo in 1994, including the market-place shelling as well as the shelling incident in Dobrinja the day before that; meetings and negotiations to achieve a cease-fire and implement and establish the total exclusion zone; the situation in and relating to Gorazde in April 1994; the detention of UN peacekeepers and UNMOs following the air-strikes that month. And let me just consult my notes for a minute. I think I've covered everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before she proceeds, just so I can make sure I make a good record for this issue because I was not -- I hadn't read the Appeals Chamber decision recently when I made my arguments to you, and I was somehow flailing around with using my instincts more than my jurisprudence. But it's our position that the Prosecution -- that to ask questions on these topics would constitute fresh evidence, and the fresh evidence decided by the Appeals Chamber was limited to documents. So we recognise that. But the issue wasn't raised directly in the Prlic case about whether or not eliciting evidence on topics of which the Prosecution was aware and which the Prosecution had the evidence would constitute fresh evidence in the form of questions to witnesses. And in this case, as you've seen from the 1997 interview that the Prosecution displayed at the beginning of its cross-examination, the Prosecution had all of this information in its possession well before it commenced its own case against Dr. Karadzic and could have called that witness and elicited all of that evidence in its case in chief. And in the Prlic Trial Chamber decision they talked about that the exception under Rule 90(H) is explained by the fact that during the Prosecution's case in chief it doesn't know which witnesses the Defence are going to call, and therefore it's perhaps unaware that these witnesses exist and don't know whether they will be in a position to testify on matters related to its case. And the Trial Chamber said therefore that if during the testimony of a Defence witness it becomes apparent that the witness has the requisite knowledge to answer the Prosecution's questions, it would therefore be justified to permit the Prosecution to address matters related to its case with that witness. And that part of the decision was not appealed. So the issue that I just want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands and what we're trying to say is that: We believe under these circumstances where the Prosecution had all this information back in 1997, that it's -- should not be allowed to elicit fresh evidence from this witness whether in the form of questions or documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I said, Mr. Robinson, in the ruling that I just gave is that if the fresh evidence affects the rights of the accused, the Chamber would deal with it on a case-by-case basis. But what you are arguing now is that fresh evidence should be banned in its totality. Is it the case, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not at all, Mr. President. In fact, I'm asking you to follow the jurisprudence on fresh evidence with respect to oral testimony as well as to documentary evidence. And the jurisprudence is that the first inquiry about fresh evidence is whether the party could have with reasonable diligence identified that evidence and presented it in its case in chief. So with respect to the item that she -- the specific items that she's mentioned, and we can start with the 1993 events in Konjevic Polje, that evidence was available to the Prosecutor, they had identified it, and they could have presented it in its case in chief, and therefore that evidence should be excluded as well as any other items contained within the witness interview from 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In case of oral testimony, how do you read "fresh evidence"? If it is not covered by the witness on the stand in its evidence in chief, do you find anything would fall under fresh evidence even if it was covered by other witnesses or dealt with by exhibits that were already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think if it came from this particular witness and it dealt with other -- things other than credibility or what was covered in his direct examination, that it would constitute fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton -- oh, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just Ms. Edgerton -- and I don't want to pre-empt what the Court had in mind, was that to proceed or to respond to Mr. Robinson's argument? Because I'm only rising for the latter purpose obviously, and if the Court had something different in mind I don't want to misunderstand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber wanted to hear from the Prosecution in response to Mr. Robinson's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. Well, I would note preliminarily, Mr. President, that when the Prosecution rose after a break in a discussion to expand on the argument made, it was deemed by Mr. Robinson to be a motion for reconsideration and to rise to the level of a higher standard, and that was partially the basis, if not wholly the basis, for the ruling that ensued. And now we see, as mentioned previously, another reversal of the Defence position. In connection with this broader issue about what the Prosecution should or should not have adduced, I think it's important to remind the Court about a position taken by the Pre-Trial Chamber in this case, specifically by Judge Bonomy, in the face of the refusal by the Defence to file a pre-trial brief or to otherwise comply with the Rules in letting the Prosecution know what the Defence case would consist of and what issues should be addressed accordingly. And Judge Bonomy said he's not -- he wasn't going to order the Defence to file a pre-trial brief because he thought that might end up being a somewhat nugatory act. But instead he would be extremely flexible and lenient in allowing the Prosecution to adduce evidence during the course of the entirety of the case that addressed issues that were relevant to the case. And I can -- the President may recall that exchange, but of course I can draw it out if necessary. The Prlic case, in essence, talks about any tension between 89(C) and 89(D) in attempting to strike a balance of fairness, in attempting to prevent on the one hand a potential "ambush" by the Prosecution; and on the other hand a bizarrely selective eliciting of evidence by the Defence calling a witness and asking him about one narrow portion when that -- one narrow portion that advances the Defence case when that witness may have a huge amount of evidence relevant to the entirety of the case that would be precluded by this tactical expedient, which is clearly not envisioned by the Rules. I would note further that cases that followed the Prlic decision, including Stanisic and Simatovic and Stanisic/Zupljanin, Prlic, and others have emphasized, among other things, the enormous size and complexity of these cases, the interest of the Trial Chamber in effective truth-finding, and have essentially found - as this Trial Chamber ruled when it returned from the break - that a Trial Chamber should essentially strike an appropriate balance on a case-by-case basis between the interests of 89(C) and (D). All of the subsequent jurisprudence is indeed consistent with the position taken by this Chamber and nothing Mr. Robinson said changes that, even if this wasn't - as he has previously characterised it - a motion for reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- the Chamber sees no reason to alter its ruling. Shall we proceed? Do we need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I have one objection to this and is that the Prosecution should not be allowed to ask leading questions when eliciting evidence for its own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm -- I have to turn to Mr. Tieger because I have to think of something on this one, Your Honours. Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can point out, as the Court is aware, that it simply was not the practice during the Prosecution case when the accused led large amounts of evidence under 90(H) through witnesses clearly identified with and friendly to the Defence, where such a matter would be of even greater concern. So I think that's a belated approach by the Defence which is tactical in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I -- there's also jurisprudence of this from the Prlic case, a decision on the mode of interrogating witnesses May 10th of 2007 at paragraph 13, and also a decision on Prosecution motion on use of leading questions on 4th of July, 2008. And in the Stanisic and Simatovic case, decision on submissions by Stanisic Defence regarding Prosecution's Rule 90(H)(ii) obligations, 12 June 2012 at paragraph 11, and I believe the jurisprudence is that they're not allowed to -- "when eliciting evidence beyond the scope of direct examination for the party's own case leading questions are not permitted."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's extremely interesting that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, we often forget to put a pause between the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I find it extremely interesting that Mr. Robinson is able to cite this jurisprudence and is aware of it when just a moment ago he was arguing that the Prosecution had no right to do the very same thing, that is, elicit the evidence that he's citing here now. That's a little -- that's just a preliminary matter. But none of those cases dealt with the fact that the -- as far as I can tell, that the Defence was permitted and with -- sought to and in the face of repeated objections about leading in various forms, engage in precisely this practice, which is the issue here, the practice of this particular case. The Defence in this case wants the benefit of having it both ways; that should not be permitted. That was not the ruling in that case. Had they been prepared to abide by the jurisprudence they cite now and the principles annunciated in those cases, it might be a different matter, but that's not the practice as in the practice of this particular case as established by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is a shame that this procedure part of the debate has been taking place in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As compromise, Ms. Edgerton, could you conduct your cross-examination in a not-leading way in the meantime and the Chamber will issue its decision in due course. As a professional I think you are capable of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. I -- I'll just try and keep an eye on the clock. It's going to take longer, I suspect, than the allotted time, but I'll move with as much alacrity as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Ms. Edgerton, the time that -- it will necessarily have to be extended bearing in mind the rather extraordinary circumstances, so I wouldn't worry for myself too much about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I endorse that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And keeping in mind what Dr. Karadzic raised while Your Honours were deliberating, I wonder if we may lift from page 37, line 7, in fact, to right now, from private session. We've been in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, and Mr. Robinson could have informed the Chamber of the need to go back -- going back to the open session at the time, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, can I just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are in open session, bear in mind that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is of course a personal diary that was never intended to be released, and so the nature of the writing is such that it's -- it was for my own personal use, so please bear that in mind when we go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got no issues with the diary being released, but it's just that it was written as a diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are not broadcasting this nor are we releasing this. We are -- what we are going to have in public session is to hear debate as to the manner in which the cross-examination is to be conducted. So where were we? For the benefit of the public, could you repeat the crux of your objection, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. During the cross-examination the Prosecution had put to the witness or put in front of the witness his diary and directed his attention to a particular portion of that diary, and we objected to the use of the diary because under the Prlic Appeals Chamber decision we believe that the use of documents during cross-examination on an area that is outside of the scope of direct examination and not related to the credibility of the witnesses must be evaluated under the test for fresh evidence. And in this case, that test requires that this evidence had not have been available to the Prosecution to introduce in its own case through the exercise of due diligence. And so therefore we believe that the diary ought not to be used either as an exhibit or as being put before the witness and being the subject of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now you understand, French interpretation has just been completed. So we have to put this much a pause between the question and the answer. Yes, Ms. Edgerton or Mr. Tieger. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to put it as simply as possible. The underlying purpose of all of the procedural Rules at this institution is to advance fairness and efficiency and to balance those two when necessary, as Mr. Robinson should be aware. I won't revert back to my -- I know in this instance, pending a resolution of the arguments made before, we are eliciting evidence in a non-leading fashion, but the expedient that Mr. Robinson is proposing at this moment in this particular case seems to me much more akin to a use of the -- of any principles annunciated in previous cases, as how many angels dance on the head of a pin. The Defence initiated the use of this diary, has introduced portions of this diary. There's no question, it seems to me, that this witness is trying to be as balanced as possible to both parties in the proceedings and to give as much useful information to the Court as possible. He's had a chance to review the diary previously. In balancing the interests of efficiency and fairness here, it's difficult to see -- it's easy to see how efficiency can be lost by an artificial approach to questions related to information that this witness has recently seen and is memorialised in his diary, and difficult to see how given the nature of the witness and the nature of the circumstances in which the diary was presented to this Court by the Defence, that there's any loss of fairness. So I would think, you know, it's simpler and completely fair to allow in this circumstance a reasonable use of the diary in the manner that Ms. Edgerton suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the most expedient thing if we're talking about expediency is for her to ask questions about the events without reference to the diary and see if it's necessary to use the diary. She did exactly what everybody's been telling Dr. Karadzic not to do, is to show a witness a document and ask a leading question about it. So maybe if we just revert to the form and see if she can get the same information without using the diary, we can avoid you having to rule on the legal issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Following the compromise we made earlier on, pending the ruling of the Chamber on the manner in which the conduct of cross-examination with respect to subject matter that was not covered by the evidence in chief, I would advise Ms. Edgerton to follow the suggestion made by Mr. Robinson in the meantime. Let's proceed. We need to go back to private session then, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we will. I just need to find my bearings again, Your Honour. I'm not quite sure I know where we're at right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could we move back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your written evidence in this case at paragraph 6 you said you found it highly unusual that the Serbs would have fired a single round at the market-place and said that normally they fired several rounds when trying to hit a target with their mortars. Now, my question is: Having come to Sarajevo only some short number of days prior to that, and in the face of what this Chamber has heard as probably the most effective cease-fire of the war following the incident, I wonder if you could tell us what your basis is for this assertion?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: A mortar is an indirect fire weapon, so it's not direct fire. The firer on the whole can't see the target, and therefore -- because it's susceptible to a number of factors, atmospherics, lack of sight, the actual target before it is hit has to be -- has to be ranged in on and fire then accurately brought to bear on to that target itself. Before a mortar can be fired, it needs to be bedded in, so that would normally take one or two mortar rounds fired before it can actually fire in any direction. Mortars on the whole are deployed in up to six mortars in a battery, quite often we would deploy three. The kill zone of a mortar which, i.e., the effective area where it could achieve its effect would be something like 30 or 40 mortars. And so mortars would be placed at distances of 30 to 40 metres to be able to achieve an area of destruction of around 100, 120 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I can just stop you there for one second, to go back to my question and what you said. You said that normally the Serbs fired several rounds when trying to hit a target with their mortars.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have experience of this happening on which you base that answer?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I physically, as I testified earlier, have been on the receiving end of it. And the day before, according to my notes, five mortar rounds were fired in order to hit that target.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So that clarifies things. So your assertion is on the basis of your experiences during an earlier posting in Bosnia and Herzegovina and your observations of an incident the day before the one we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: And obviously throughout the time that we arrived in Sarajevo we'd constantly heard artillery mortar fire, so it's common practice -- you can't with a mortar see a target and expect to hit it with a single round, and if you did it would be extremely lucky.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that -- your indulgence for a moment. Throughout the time that you arrived in Sarajevo you constantly heard artillery mortar fire. Was that still the case following the cease-fire of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The actual cease-fire having had the meeting with the Bosnian Serb army and the government forces in Sarajevo established a cease-fire and the very next day -- on the day of the cease-fire itself, there were breaches of the cease-fire. I think it was on the 11th of February, if I recall - I might be wrong - with small arms fire in the morning, small arms fire throughout the day, and then mortar fire that evening, all of which were perpetrated by the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you told us during our meeting on the 7th of February that you've not had experience commanding mortar or artillery units; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you do have some knowledge of the use of mortars. I wonder if you could tell us what you understand harassing fire to be in military terms?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Harassing fire is basically fire that's directed towards an enemy designed to cause them inconvenience, to prevent them from establishing their mission in terms of doing what they want to do, breaking up their forces. It's not designed to be accurate in terms of hitting targets themselves, but there is the possibility that they could achieve the same effect if they hit them. So it's basically a means of breaking up or disrupting an enemy force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would it also be intended to undermine morale, for example?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. If you're under mortar artillery fire, your morale's pretty low, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Increase the enemy's stress levels then?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Deny them the opportunity for things like sleep or rest and, like you've just alluded to, probably resupply?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's all that. That's, regrettably, the nature of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you see that happening during your tour in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Throughout the -- we weren't there that long before the cease-fire was signed, and therefore we could -- I could only cite what we saw from the 14th of January through to when the cease-fire itself was signed following the meeting at the airport on the 9th of February. So there was sporadic fire taking place throughout the city, but, you know, I must stress that it wasn't simply one-way. There was outgoing fire, there was incoming fire, you know, and as I've mentioned certainly after the cease-fire was signed all the fire was outgoing. So there was a siege taking place and the aim of a siege is to force the -- those besieged to come to terms in terms of capitulate or surrender. The Bosnian government clearly wished the siege to have an effect whereby the siege would be broken not by their own forces, because they couldn't do that physically themselves, but for Western intervention, and by delivering aid to the people we achieved a status in Sarajevo where people were kept alive. And so regrettably the siege was prolonged, and as the siege went on from 1992 through to the cease-fire, it was the people who suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just talked about the Bosnian government's -- what you felt to be the Bosnian government's wishes in respect of the siege. Are you in a position to comment similarly on what you felt to be the Bosnian Serb government's objectives as regards the siege?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb objective would have been to contain the 1st ARBiH Corps in Sarajevo, to neutralise it so it wouldn't create problems for it, and then force the Bosnian government to the negotiating table, whereby I suppose a long-term peace negotiation settlement for the future of Bosnia could be worked out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A peace negotiation that would have given them a portion of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I imagine it's part of an overall settlement for, you know, what they intend to do in terms of establishing Republika Srpska as a state within a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was just to ask or to be reminded of what time Your Honours had indicated you might take the next break, and we're right around that time I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to have a break now, but for planning purposes could I ask you how much longer you would need -- I'm asking whether we need to release the next witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rough -- roughly?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's actually touch and go I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You spent an hour so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have half an hour more from the allotted time, but I think you may need a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well -- indeed, yes, Your Honour, so I'm trying to -- I have to take some time to recover my balance now, and I'm just trying to estimate. I'm not sure yet that you should release the next witness, but after the lunch break, immediately after the lunch break, I would be able to confirm. Would that be sufficient ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fine. I take it Mr. Karadzic also needs some time for his re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, well then, no question, Your Honours, I'm quite sure that the next witness can be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Nabilah Reza from the Australian National University in Canberra who is one of our legal interns and working on our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if it hasn't already been instructed, the next witness can definitely be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Edgerton, we would like to conclude this witness's evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will do my utmost, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how long would you need to conclude your cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope I can be -- not -- understanding I am to not lead him, I fully expect I would take another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could try to conclude in three-quarters of an hour, try your best.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, we left off talking about the Markale I incident and going back to that you said in your statement to Dr. Karadzic's Defence that it appeared that the shell would have had to come in with a very high trajectory, suggesting that it had been fired at a close range. Now, is this information that you received from Major Russell, who you also referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: When we visited the site ourselves, the close proximity of the tall buildings to where the explosion had taken place was clearly, you know, very close to those buildings. And so all the reporting from the various sources including Major Russell was that if it was fired from the direction that we understood it to be fired from, from roughly the north/north-east, that it had to be fired at very close range in order to achieve the elevation, I'm no expert, the elevation, then to come down so close to the building. When we heard, in terms of the numbers of casualties, we were shocked that a single mortar could deliver that much devastation in terms of 69 killed, nearly 200 wounded. But of course if it was a tightly packed market-place, then that would be probably understandable. And again, the view at the time was when one looks at the market square it was almost look a hollow square where you have four parts to it but one was exposed to the road so if a mortar was to be fired to directly hit the market-place, from our perspective it should have been fired potentially from the south in order to have a better chance of hitting it as opposed to the north-east at closer range. It didn't make sense why a mortar would be fired at that market place from the north-east given the potential obstacles to its flight if it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now let's just -- on the subject of trajectory, I want to deal with that for a moment. Because you have some knowledge of mortars, I assume you know that mortars can fire on up to six charges?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct, but then the charges themselves are designed to overlap in terms of range. So it's down to firer's experience to work out the number of charges to the elevation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you know, I would assume, that as the charges increase the distance range of the mortar also increases then?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: To achieve its maximum range, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You -- do you recall confirming during our interview in January that you can't read a mortar firing table?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I'm an anti-tank officer of old. I'm not a mortar man.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Major Russell actually came here to testify, and he was shown a firing table for the type of mortar that was launched on the market-place that day, and he was shown that the angle of descent for each successive charge remained almost the same. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you wouldn't know then that on seeing this firing table, he agreed that he had applied an erroneous principle at the time of the incident and come to an incorrect conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's T-29439 to 29440 for the record. And still with regard to Major Russell, even though -- who you described as an artillery officer in paragraph 8, did you know that up until the point of this incident he told this Chamber he'd conducted only five crater analyses?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's five more than I ever have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's T-29382. And in your evidence you also refer to his remark that the shrapnel and other physical evidence on the scene had been swept away and that was suspicious, so I assume then that you don't know that before Major Russell went to the scene there had already been a number of investigations on the site?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: We didn't know that in terms of -- in term of recollection, but we assume it would have happened. It's just that when he mentioned it, he said there was no evidence in terms of physical evidence on the ground to suggest what type of mortar explosion it was, which then added to the whole theory of conspiracies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, you wouldn't know then, based on what you've said, that the tail fin of the mortar in this case was actually recovered before Major Russell visited the scene?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I've never seen that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were you aware of the fact that a subsequent technical investigation into this incident was ordered and carried out by a team from UNHQ in Zagreb later on that month?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: We were aware and we understand -- as I understand the deduction was that it could have been fired from either side of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now finally with respect to paragraph 9 of your written evidence and the report that the mortar might have been fired by a Mujahedin group who had allegedly missed the target when trying to kill Jews leaving the city, do you remember confirming during our meeting in January that the actual only time you had ever heard of the Mujahedin being physically active in Bosnia was around Maglaj?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct. Immediately after the incident took place when the information started coming through, filtering through, there was various reporting going on. One was that it could have been dropped from the top of the building, one that it was Mujahedin, and of course these were just report. We'd never seen Mujahedin in Sarajevo or in resembling in and around Sarajevo, so it was another possible to solution to how this could have happened, but then after that report we heard nothing more about it. And to be honest with you, in terms of General Rose himself and the headquarters, we weren't really interested ourselves who did it. We just made sure that this, you know, this tragedy resulted in an opportunity where we could basically do something positive and use that crisis, as I think Mr. Akashi said, you know, using mandarin and Chinese, that every crisis has two meanings: Danger and opportunity. And what we were absolutely keen about wasn't -- using this as an opportunity to bring the two sides together in order to end this madness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, French translation has only now been completed. Both of you are kindly requested by the interpreters to put pause and to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, and my apologies to my colleagues and thanks for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This -- to move on, this opportunity and the cease-fire that resulted from the incident, could you tell us what the reaction was of the civilian population in the city to the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's quite difficult question to answer because -- even before the cease-fire was signed we would quite often use opportunity to walk from the residency to the Presidency for various meetings and meet people. But clearly when the cease-fire was signed, it was almost as if a huge yoke had been lifted off their shoulders and people came out onto the streets in an attempt to go about normal business that they'd not been able to do for the last two years, and again that was on both sides of the divide. So, you know, the people in Sarajevo didn't want this war, you know, they wanted it to end as much as we did clearly. And then there was new hope in Sarajevo at the time because, you know, there was a huge clamour to end this -- as I said, everybody was blaming the Serbs, even though we had our definite doubts. And of course there was this huge pressure to start bombing the Serbs either to the negotiating table or out of Sarajevo. So immediately after the cease-fire was signed it still wasn't over because the airport agreements had a cease-fire and then a period of time to allow the Bosnian Serbs and the government forces to withdraw their heavy weaponry. And if that wasn't achieved, then the air campaign would then begin. And so immediately there was huge, obviously, adulation of the people, but we then had this period where we just didn't know which way it was going to go, either, you know, an opportunity or it would be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- now, well, then, to move on into that area, I take it from what you've just said that you were involved in negotiations with respect to the establishment of the cease-fire and the definition and implementation of the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you -- in your statement you refer to a meeting with Bosnian authorities on the 8th of February, and just to put this in context, perhaps you could tell us about meetings that might have occurred earlier in that day.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: It was clearly after the incident a whole series of meetings. And on the -- prior to going to see the Bosnians in the -- in the parliament building, General Rose had already been to Belgrade in order to identify what we could do, and then we were then -- we arranged a meeting in Lukavica, where we believed -- we already understood that General Mladic (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: (redacted) As soon as we knew the Serbs were willing to meet the very next day to have the meeting, we then drove to the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo, where General Divjak was there as well as General Hajrulahovic, Hajrulahovic who was the chief of military intelligence and Colonel Dakic. And we then said to them that the Serbs were willing to come to the negotiating table. They had agreed to all the terms that we proposed to them. But they were reluctant to agree to anything unless effectively political arrangements for a total peace was to be signed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I can just stop you there for a moment so we can allow for the French interpretation to catch up. Thank you. Now, just to put that meeting -- to put the meeting, this meeting with Bosnian officials that you referred to in further context, I take it from what you've just said that the surprise that General Rose sprung on them that you referred to in paragraph 11 of your statement was made in the context of their reluctance to sign up to the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton, I leave it to you as well as Mr. Witness, what to hear in public session and what to hear in private session. I'm just telling you as a reminder. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think - and thank you for that. I think that from lines on page 80, line 21 up until page -- your indulgence for a moment. Up until page 81, line 7, at the end of the sentence that says -- that ends with the word "terms," perhaps that should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we could maybe do that for now, but this is also included in the statement so we may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is in under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, even in the summary, though, I think there was some mention of this meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- but we can be refining it later if necessary. Out of an abundance of caution, if we do redact it, it's okay for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In the summary, I don't think Mr. Karadzic referred to the participants by name. Yes, we'll do that, Ms. Edgerton, and in the meantime please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the meeting with General Milovanovic was not part of this earlier evidence as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to another paragraph of your Defence statement and that's the meeting mentioned at paragraph 13, where you say: "When the Bosnian military delegation refused to take part in meetings to arrange a cease-fire, General Rose once again met with the government leadership and told them that unless they participated he would tell the world what he suspected about the shellings of the market-place." I just want to ask you to clarify: Were you actually at this meeting where General Rose said this or not?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: There was two meetings. We all arrived at the airport --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I can just caution you. If you think your answer should be given in private session, feel free to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Okay. There was two meetings. We were all at the airport anticipating both sides to arrive to start negotiations. As had been promised, the Bosnian Serb delegation had arrived led by General (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, if I could stop the witness there and ask for private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And a redaction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I'll ask the question again. So in terms of the UNMOs and UN peacekeepers who were not in base, if I can call it that, what was the Bosnian Serb reaction?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: As far as the Bosnian Serbs were concerned following the air-strikes, we'd now taken sides against them in support of the Bosnian Muslims, and so not only was there a huge anger on the Bosnian Serb leadership's part for us carrying out these air-strikes, but then their soldiers effectively encircled the weapons collection points, there was threats of once again taking over those weapons, and UNMOs and soldiers in isolated locations were then surrounded and basically detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you learn from any member of the Bosnian Serb leadership under whose direction that operation had taken place?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: No. I mean, we could only assume that because the leadership was so angry about the air-strikes that it would have come from either Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic because they now viewed us as no longer being impartial.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was the -- did you -- did the General have concerns for the safety of the UNMOs and peacekeepers who had been so detained?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was in the forefront of General Rose's mind, and of course while this was all going on the attacks against Gorazde were still taking place. And we then had cause to carry out more air-strikes against the Bosnian Serb tanks and soldiers who were advancing towards Gorazde itself. As soon as the air-strikes had effectively started, it was at that point that we also had all our relations with the Bosnian Serb leadership completely suspended, which required then Dr. Owen and Stoltenberg to fly into Sarajevo, for them to try and, you know, repair relations between the international community and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what were the General's concerns for their safety?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Just in case something happened to them. At the end of the day, you know, this was -- we had now gone from opportunity in a crisis to danger and, you know, General Rose was absolutely adamant that what he wasn't going to do was stop any air-strikes that needed to be carried out just because we had soldiers detained. You know, the two things were linked but were to be dealt with separately. And so General Rose was adamant that the air-strikes would continue, and eventually, you know, as a result of the air-strikes, as a result of the negotiations that were taking place at a much higher level, the Bosnian Serb attack against Gorazde ended and were able to resolve that crisis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one final question to go back to Sarajevo, over the course of your tour there, did you -- and your conversations with civilians in the city, did you understand the conditions to have any psychological effect on them?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Absolutely. At the end of the day, if you are subjected - it doesn't matter who you are, where you live - to the threat or the physical firing of small arms ammunitions from machine-guns or sniper rifles to mortars to heavy artillery to tank ammunition, if that was always hanging over you, psychologically, you know, that would be damaging. That's the nature of warfare and regrettably siege warfare as we witnessed in Sarajevo and as we've seen in conflicts more recently in Iraq and Afghanistan, where you fight amongst the people. Yes, you are primarily targeting the military, but the civilians regrettably tend to bear the greatest burden.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to go back before closing actually to one point that you've just made with respect to -- or the issue we were just discussing with respect to the detention of the UN peacekeepers and the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at this point, Your Honours, I would like to invite the witness to turn to his diary. And it's 65 ter 24422.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to ask you to have a look at the entries for 14 April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think there has to be a question first before doing this to establish that it's necessary for him to refresh his memory or some other legitimate use of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the modality we are -- talked about, but, Mr. Witness has looked at his diary already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he's done that when it was necessary to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I don't -- this is a leading question, obviously, as you've told Dr. Karadzic many times, putting a document before the witness before asking a question is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we agreed, or at least I told the parties to follow that proceedings or regime, but -- sir, have you read the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He has read the diary already. So what is your question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I could have rephrased the question, and I apologise, but the question is:

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you described these UN personnel as being detained, but I note that on page 50 in the third and fourth paragraph you used the word "hostage," saying this was potentially a hostage situation. And at page 55 and page 56 you also used the term "hostage" to describe their status. And yet you haven't used that word now and I'm wondering why.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I mean, we talk about detention, they're detainees. A hostage is exactly what they were in that respect in terms of they were being held in order to elicit a deal or something as a result, the idea being, you know, the Bosnian Serbs deliberately took these people because they believed that we were now enemies because we'd bombed them, with a view that if the bombings continued that potentially something might happen to them. I don't use the term -- I use the term "hostage" in my diary, I didn't use it then, there was no reason why I shouldn't have used it, but there was no malicious intent intended.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to Mr. Karadzic for his re-examination, could we go back to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Mr. Karadzic, I'd like to know for planning purposes how long you would need to conclude your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until when do we work today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Originally we are to adjourn at quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to finish by then, but I would beg for a bit of flexibility, perhaps until 3.00? But I hope I will finish before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start with last things first. Witness, according to what you know, was the NATO air force precise in shelling the Serbian positions near Gorazde? Were there any hits, in other words?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, how --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did raise the subject of the air-strikes generally, but this I think goes far outside what I did raise in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, Mr. Karadzic, how it arose from Ms. Edgerton's cross-examination in terms of precision of NATO strike?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm going to reveal more than I wanted. How precise were they? Were there any persons who guided the shelling? Were there hostages or were there prisoners? Please trust me with that. I know what I'm aiming for, but I don't want to put leading questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The NATO air-strikes on Gorazde conducted over what was very difficult terrain. Anybody's who's been to Gorazde will know how difficult it is moving very quickly in terms of the flight path to engage potentially moving or static targets. The NATO aircraft were clearly doing a number of overflights, taking reconnaissance images of known Bosnian Serb positions, but we also had the capability because of the forces in terms of the Joint Commission observers to direct fire directly onto targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, there were people on the ground and they took an active part in the shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The nature of the quality of the Joint Commission observers meant that they could revert from, as soldiers, a peacekeeping role to a war fighting role. So as soon as we were in a position because of the UN Security Council Resolution 836 to use self-defence or force to protect the safe areas, General Rose then directed that that action take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an occasion to see me personally requesting that a distinction be established between close air support and air-strikes? We accepted close air support but we did not want air-strikes. We actually thought that air-strikes would be a direct involvement and interference in the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you feeding the witness with answers? Could you reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago you stated that General Rose thought that [In English] self-defence or force to protect the safe areas. [Interpretation] Was it part of your mandate to militarily protect the protected areas? I'm not -- I'm talking about your forces. Was it part of your mandate to take an active part in the war in case protected areas came under attack?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: General Rose interpreted this as part of UN Security Council Resolution 836. Close air support would be in direct support of or in defence of our own forces.
