Air-strikes were targeted against Bosnian Serb tanks, observation posts, artillery, and forces to prevent them from further advancing into Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a while ago you stated that in Serbian perception you became their enemy. What would you call a member of an enemy formation who was captured? Would he be a hostage or would he be a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: In the state of war in the regard that you describe, then it would be a prisoner. But we didn't see ourselves as being at war with the Bosnian Serb people. And throughout this whole process on the telephone to General Mladic and other leaders, one thing I had to confirm on every occasion that we weren't taking sides and we were, therefore, only doing this in re post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the Serbian people did not perceive you in that way; however, how did the Serbian army perceived you in view of the NATO air-strikes which were directed by soldiers who were on the ground? Did they perceive you as an enemy?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic is talking about something that is, I think, a year outside of this witness's tour of duty and was not part of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only comment about the air-strikes in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the basis? You say that it's a year outside?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: NATO air-strikes were in September 1995, August/September 1995, and not in 1994, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He talked about the detention of UNMOs, Ms. Edgerton. What year was it, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the issue is that Dr. Karadzic views the use of force in Gorazde to prevent the Bosnian Serb army entering the town as air-strikes or we're using that term. What the Prosecution are suggesting is actually in 1994 that was termed close air support, whereas the actual air-strikes were in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But to answer the question, obviously, the Bosnian Serb military were not happy with the fact that we had started bombing them and very much viewed us as the aggressor and viewed us as an enemy at that time, which is something that we didn't perceive ourselves to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the relationship between the Bosnian Serb and UNPROFOR develop after the air-strikes in Gorazde? And I am talking about both military and political authorities on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Initially all our relationships with both the military and the political leadership were completely severed, and then over time through the work of Owen Stoltenberg we were able very quickly to re-establish civilian-only communications channels with Dr. Karadzic. There was no military -- there was no formal military negotiations take place. A whole series of meetings then took place between Yasushi Akashi and Dr. Karadzic in an attempt to resolve the crisis. At the forefront of everybody's mind was to end the hostage situation with, as we referred it, or the detainees or the prisoners. And Dr. Karadzic was very supportive of that. And this is where we then had arguments between Dr. Karadzic and the military. The military weren't keen to release these individuals, whereas Dr. Karadzic - realising how this was being perceived and broadcast around the world - was very keen to end the crisis. The formal military negotiations only then took place once the air-strikes, close air support, had been concluded, we were then able to implement the agreement to formally establish a cease-fire and exclusion zone in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to what Madam Edgerton said about air-strikes in 1994 and in 1995, how many air-strikes, NATO air-strikes, in Bosnia there were against the Serbs there, was it just once or was it more than once?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to clarify things. Madam Edgerton thought that I was talking about hostages which were taken in 1995 and we are talking about air-strikes that happened near Gorazde in 1994, and in 1994 there were more air-strikes, not only those in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber allows the question to be put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a number of air-strikes or planned missions against various targets in Bosnia at that time. In fact, the first mission that we intended to conduct was actually against the Bosnian Croats, with -- a few of them who were holding up a convoy further to the south of Sarajevo, but then word got the out to the Croats that we were intending to do this, probably from our own headquarters, and that mission was called off. Over Gorazde, off the top of my head I think we carried out five, maybe six separate missions, and there was an aborted mission also in Bihac when the Serbs around the same time again were responding to incidents in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did UNPROFOR request missions to be carried out against the Muslim army and how many times was that implemented, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this relevant to cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if I can just address that. The Prosecution elicited how angry the Bosnian Serbs were concerning the air-strikes that were directed against them. I think this is a legitimate element of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, let me understand you, Mr. Robinson. You're saying that part of the anger might have been because they did not perceive that there were strikes carried out against the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly, that they were targeted unfairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At no stage were air-strikes or any sort of offensive action targeted against the Bosnian Muslims for any of the breaches that they conducted anywhere around Bosnia, irrespective of on the front line or a safe area. And politically it wouldn't have been sanctioned because, of course, whilst General Rose could request the air-strikes, ultimately it was a NATO mission that would be called to support his request. And we viewed that politically this would be unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall leave this subject now. I will not talk about a particular occasion, but you did confirm that you had an opportunity to review the situation in Dobrinja. In Dobrinja, did you notice any presence of the BH army, trenches, installations, artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: There was a brigade of the 1st Sarajevo Corps based in Dobrinja, so needless to say that the forward edges of the -- of the area were for the trenches and they had obviously small arms to the fore, and in amongst the rear they had their mortars and other heavy weaponry, so they were operating monastery the people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have said earlier today that it was in the interest of the Muslim side for fighting to continue and for the situation to look as bad as possible for the purpose of involving NATO and the West generally into the war on their side. As far as the fighting in Sarajevo is concerned and the demilitarisation of Sarajevo, what were the interests of Serbs in that area? And what position did General Milovanovic take concerning this crisis and concerning the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: General Milovanovic had the full authority from yourself and General Mladic to come to an agreement with us to formally end the conflict in and around Sarajevo without any caveats on that agreement. I -- we all knew that from a, you know, Bosnian Serb perspective, the ongoing siege around Sarajevo and the fact that there was artillery, mortars, machine-guns, sniper fire taking place was doing their cause horrendous damage, which is why one thing that annoyed General Rose was the fact that the Bosnian government side resisted all our attempts to try and end this. And so that's why the opportunity of the market massacre was such that we were now in a position with the Serbs under pressure from air-strikes, because they were being blamed for this, and with the Bosnian government being under pressure to act because we effectively fought them to a corner, we therefore had the opportunity to finally end the destruction that was taking place in Gorazde -- wrong, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 7 on this page you mention horrendous damage. How did the general fighting in Sarajevo impact on the interests of Serbs and the Serbs' position, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I mean, it's obvious that the Bosnian Serb population in the suburbs, places like Gorazde, Vogosca, Ilidza, they themselves had been subjected to fire from the Bosnian side. But at the end of the day, the amount of fire directed the other way was far greater than the fire directed towards the Bosnian Serb side. If you're under fire, you're under fire, you still live under the same psychological or threatening conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know how far the confrontation lines were from each other and what the situation was on the hills around Sarajevo vis-a-vis the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The confrontation line was very different depending on where you went. In places around Ilidza, the confrontation line at some stage could be as far away as a hundred metres away from each other through to, when we visited one position, 5 metres. Places around Grbavica in one case just to the east of Grbavica there was a building known as the red house, and they were literally separated by only a wall within the same building. Further away, out of -- once we left the built-up area of Sarajevo and then you went into open ground, because it would have been suicidal for any of the sides to fight in open ground, the Bosnian Serb line was then further to the rear where they obviously could dominate the ground and dominate -- or prevent any infantry assaults, of which were there many, in the period that we were there before the cease-fire with their superior heavy weaponry. So, you know, the front line could have been as close as one, you know, 1 foot through to, you know, 1 kilometre, in terms of the difference between the two forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the BH army have its own positions on those same hills around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I don't recall them dominating any high ground around Sarajevo, but there was high ground within Sarajevo that they had their positions on. Obviously then immediately around Sarajevo you then had a mixture of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslim positions. The only time we were aware of any mortars being fired from the area of -- the other side of the airport into Sarajevo was on one particular day when our prime minister was visiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which side fired that day a mortar?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Bosnian government forces fired on that day. One of the trends that we very quickly realised was taking place in Sarajevo was whenever there was any high-level negotiations or business taking place, then the Bosnian government side quite frequently would fire mortars, let's say from the rear of where we were towards the Presidency or in this case from their controlled area to the west of Sarajevo into Sarajevo, with a view of -- well, provoking Serb fire. And of course, you know, whenever we had a high-ranking visitor, they would hear the fire going on, a news reporter was there, and, of course, on the whole, just where I suspect your question is leading me, on the whole this was reported in the media. But of course it was always reported as the Serbs firing at the time of this visit as opposed to being provoked, which was what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You were asked on page 71 about harassing fire and the types of harassment against an enemy aimed at lowering his combat morale, et cetera. Are these unlawful war methods or are they allowed?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Under the normal rules of war, fire against an enemy in terms of the combatants can take a number of forms and harassing fire against enemy combatants is one of those forms which is accepted. The problem in Sarajevo was that the Bosnian government forces were located in amongst the people, and therefore inadvertently -- well, in reality we therefore had harassing fire potentially fired against the combatants. We had also had individuals who were probably deliberately targeting and were targeting civilians which in itself was psychological warfare against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would you say, on whom lies the responsibility to demilitarise a civilian area? Was the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska, bound to do that or the BH army? Who is responsible for removing their own civilians from the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's a proper question for this witness. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned - speaking of Konjevic Polje - and I'm not going to say anything specific, but you said that mines had been set and they had to be removed in order to pass through. Whose minefield was it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, we'd asked the Bosnian Serbs to remove those mines from the Zvornik Brigade. They said they weren't their mines because they didn't have the mapping in terms of how the mines were laid, they couldn't help us. So they were Bosnian government mines that we were clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned - and I'll avoid being specific again in order for us to stay in open session - that General Morillon had a time window of 12 hours in which he did not manage to complete the mission so he stayed overnight. And then on the way back the UN team had another 12 hours. Who approved the other 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The 12-hour dead-lines were agreed between the UN forces and the Bosnian Serb army in the area, i.e., we had 12 hours to complete the missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslim side, Oric and his men, know about this time allowance of 12 hours? Were they informed?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: Yes, they were informed, and therefore when the 12-hour dead-line had ended we knew therefore that at any stage after the 12 hours that the Bosnian Serbs would then recommence their attack at that stage, which is why the forces in the pocket at that time were pleading with the people who surrounded the vehicles and the soldiers who were there also, to release those soldiers in order they can get out of the pocket before the attack went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that 12 hours were granted in advance, was the renewed attack by the Republika Srpska army legitimate?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: You could argue that it was legitimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to say what's legitimate or not legitimate. How much longer do you need, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will conclude in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Witness, as regards information released to the media and to international officials, how would you assess what the Muslim side put out about Cerska, Gorazde, and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: The Bosnian government very frequently, almost in every occasion, whenever there was a crisis, would right from the beginning almost exaggerate the situation that was being faced on the ground. This was then broadcast in the media, which then put us under great pressure to act. But of course the information that we were then receiving from these places from our own people quite often contradicted those claims. But whenever we put the truth out, in reality that was already too late and the oversensationalisation of the circumstances in international media took preference. So there's, you know, there was a huge amount of disinformation taking place, and ultimately from a media perspective the media was very sided against the Serbs and very pro-Bosnian government. So, you know, the Bosnian government would use the circumstances to put pressure on the international community, particularly the Americans, to come in on side -- on their side in order to end the siege and to bomb the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last subject. You mentioned that somebody from the United Nations carried out an investigation into the incident of the 4th February 1994 in Dobrinja. Was that a French officer named Verdy who did also the 5th February analysis that was rejected by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P01597, P01597.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the one you meant? Was there one analysis or two analyses on behalf of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the witness gave the name earlier in the transcript. Second of all, the way the question is phrased is inappropriate and should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You meant the accused. I'm sorry, yes, I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, the name of the individual, the name of the officer, the witness has already provided that today in the transcript. I'll just try and find that for Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise, I believe the name of the officer was in the diary that we weren't permitted to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was whether there were one or more analysis on behalf of the United Nations; and if there was only one, was it this one? Which one did the witness refer to?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I'm only aware of the one analysis that took place and the individual who we saw at the site is the releasing officer on this form that you've got in front of me. I have a picture of the actual analysis taking place, if it helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this officer collaborate with the investigators of the Bosnian government on this job?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that whatsoever. I don't know of the officer that you refer to, I've never heard his name mentioned before. I only know the releasing officer on the actual form itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we agree -- could we scroll down a little. The angle of approach, 2.000 mils. Do you know which system was applied here, the one that has 6.000 mils or 6400 mils?

utterances.speaker: KW570
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I don't think it's a question for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you, Witness, as a military person like to see in this report also the minimal range?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure whether the witness has expertise enough to answer that kind of question. Why don't you conclude then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this same officer worked on an analysis the next day at Markale and that one was rejected by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not an appropriate question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please conclude your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will do just that after expressing my gratitude to the witness for coming here, testifying, and being prepared to stay beyond the time he expected to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the witness could be excused, there are a couple of matters I would like to deal with. Shall we draw the blinds and let the witness be excused first. That may be safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned the witness can stay and hear any of that unless it's a private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we need to go into private session. So let's draw the curtains. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has any agreement been made as regards the order of witnesses on Monday and Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, so I think we'll just stay with the present order of calling three witnesses prior to General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I should have dealt with this in private session. We will redact this. My apology. With the blinds I was mistaken. Shall we go to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. The hearing is now adjourned. We'll resume on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday the 21st day of January, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
